choice: figure-it-out at Feature steps, one owner, no fan-out
why: one module and two call sites; the change is code-coupled

choice: min(wall age, monotonic age) when the beat's boot id matches the reader's
why: monotonic stops during a suspend and advances with wall time in a hang, so a hang stays down (ac-2) and a suspend does not count (ac-1)

choice: compare boot ids from /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id; another boot is down (round 2, f-2)
why: monotonic restarts at boot, so an old stamp cannot be compared (ac-4); the box runs Linux under systemd

choice: two new columns, seen_boot TEXT and seen_monotonic REAL, added by the existing ALTER TABLE path
why: rows stay in orch.health.db (ticket constraint); older files gain the columns on first open

choice: _latest_checks takes the boot and monotonic stamp from the row with the newest last_seen
why: device-probe and dashboard-push merge rows across processes (ac-3)

choice: read_uptime returns None unless the clock is time.time
why: a fixed test wall clock cannot be paired with the real monotonic clock; existing tests keep wall-only ages

choice: orch health, orch status and the dashboard snapshot pass the reader's uptime
why: self-heal reads orch health --json; status and the dashboard show the same states

choice: poller slow-cycle age stays on wall time
why: outside the acceptance criteria; a suspend mid-cycle can still show the poller stale (not down) once

choice: a beat whose boot id differs from the reader's is down, reason '<never ...> since reboot', at any wall age
why: the process that wrote it died with that boot, so wall age cannot keep it up (ac-4); every writer runs on the box, so the boot id is the box's

choice: a beat's cleanup deletes another pid's row only when it is past DOWN_BEATS by wall age and its monotonic stamp from this boot is too
why: the cleanup used wall age alone and deleted suspend-fresh probes of other devices (ac-3); the SQL never deletes a row _age leaves fresh; it keeps an earlier-boot row until its wall age runs out, which classify already reports down. Deleting by classify instead would drop another pid's never-reached probe row at once

choice: macos check was never picked up by a hosted runner (annotation: not acquired after multiple attempts, no steps ran)
why: infrastructure, not this PR; the round-2 push reruns it

choice: once a check target has a success from this boot, its rows from an earlier boot drop out of the merge in _latest_checks; rows with no boot stamp stay
why: wall time can run backward across a reboot, so an earlier-boot row with a larger wall stamp is still older; with no current-boot success the earlier-boot row stays and f-2 keeps the target down
